quote: public image CDN
problem: Nothing in the book says what a CDN is, though it was used three times before (ch11-dns, ch11-modern, ch12-security). The prose never mentions this example either. The sighted reader sees 'not here' for repudiation and disclosure and has to work out why (nothing secret, no action anyone could later deny). That reason is only in the hidden <desc>, not in the drawn words, the caption or the strip.
fix: plain label or one clause: a server that hands anyone the site's public pictures, so nothing is secret and nobody acts there
reason: Checked the section packet and the t7.333 screenshot. 'Not here' appears on repudiation and disclosure with no reason drawn. The reason is only in the hidden desc. CDN is never defined in the book (ch11 and ch12 use it in passing). The R cell is not self-evident, since repudiation is about someone taking an action.
judge_fix: Edit the caption (ch15-mindset-p4), keeping it at two sentences: 'STRIDE turns threat modelling into six questions asked of every part of a design: could someone spoof, tamper, repudiate, disclose, deny service or elevate privilege here? The answers differ from part to part: a login service faces all six, while a server that hands out public pictures (a CDN) has nothing secret to leak and no action anyone could later deny, and each yes names the property that part must defend.' Optionally relabel the tab 'public image server'.

quote: On a data-flow diagram, processes face all six
problem: This is in the How it works strip ('Per element'). The book never teaches 'data-flow diagram', 'data stores' or 'flows'. 'Processes' here means something other than the known OS term, so a reader who opens the strip cannot follow why some elements face six threats and others three (Pass 30 flagged this and it is still there).
fix: cut the bullet, or say: in a sketch of the design, the programs, the places data rests and the arrows it travels along
reason: 'Data-flow diagram', 'processes', 'data stores' and 'flows' are never taught elsewhere in the book (grep of all parts: the only hit is this strip). 'Processes' here means a drawn box, not the OS term the reader knows, so the bullet cannot be followed.
judge_fix: Replace the 'Per element' bullet with: '*Per element.* Draw the design as boxes and arrows: the programs face all six threats, while the places where data rests and the arrows it travels along mainly face tampering, disclosure and denial.'

quote: valid for that call site when it built the program for that call site
problem: The sentence that states CFI's rule says 'for that call site' twice, so the reader stops to work out whether two different things are meant. The duplicate came in with the Pass 29 law-4 rewrite (commit 9aea00a).
fix: delete the second 'for that call site'
reason: The duplicated phrase is in the text of ch15-memory-p3 exactly as quoted.
judge_fix: 'the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program.'

quote: Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below.
problem: ch3-defenses-p9 taught that a ret is an indirect jump and that CFI checks indirect jumps, so it is the defence against ROP. Here CFI checks only indirect calls and leaves returns to other defences. The reader cannot square the two chapters, and cannot see how a check that skips returns guards against ROP, which is built from returns. The 'relatives' it actually blocks (gadgets reached through an overwritten function pointer, JOP in Fig 15.2) are never named.
fix: one clause: the CFI that compilers ship checks only calls through pointers (ROP's relatives); the returns from Chapter 3 go to the shadow stack and PAC
reason: ch3-defenses-p9 says a ret is an indirect jump and CFI records where indirect jumps may land; ch15-memory-p3 says CFI checks indirect calls and returns go to shadow stack and PAC. The two read as contradictory and the 'relatives' of ROP that CFI blocks are never named. Real, but only a clause is needed.
judge_fix: Replace 'Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below.' with: 'As compilers ship it, CFI guards only these calls through pointers, the route ROP's relatives take; the returns that ROP itself rides, which Chapter 3 also counted among indirect jumps, are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below.'

quote: ASLR | 2003+ · randomisation
problem: Fig 15.2 calls itself 'Fig 3.11 extended', yet it dates ASLR 2003+ and draws it after DEP/NX. ch3-defenses-p6 says PaX shipped ASLR in 2001, and Fig 3.11 says 2001+. Low severity; flagged before as a register flag but never ruled.
fix: owner call: 2001+ to match Fig 3.11 and the prose
reason: Fig 15.2 is a kept-original figure. The error is real: ch3-defenses-p6 says PaX shipped ASLR in 2001 and Fig 3.11 (also kept-original) draws '2001+', but Fig 15.2, which calls itself 'Fig 3.11 extended', draws '2003+'. PaX ASLR dates to 2001, so 2003 is wrong.
judge_fix: Owner call: change the Fig 15.2 label to 'ASLR | 2001+ · randomisation' (source: PaX, 2001; matches ch3-defenses-p6 and Fig 3.11).

quote: PAC · CET shadow stack | 2017+ · hardware-signed RA
problem: The CET shadow stack signs nothing. It compares a protected copy of the return address, as ch15-memory-p4 and ch3-defenses-p9 both say, so the shared label 'hardware-signed' is wrong for CET. Low severity.
fix: owner call: 'hardware-guarded return address'
reason: Fig 15.2 is a kept-original figure. Real but minor: the CET shadow stack compares a protected copy and signs nothing (ch15-memory-p4 and ch3-defenses-p9 say so). The label 'hardware-signed RA' is exact only for PAC. Fig 3.11 carries the same 'hardware-signed' wording for CFI, PAC and CET.
judge_fix: Owner call: 'PAC · CET shadow stack | 2017+ · hardware-guarded RA' (or 'hardware-protected return address').

quote: now the laptop sends every packet destined for the gateway to the attacker instead
problem: 'Gateway' first appears here (earlier the word only occurs inside 'Border Gateway Protocol'), and ch8-ethernet's ARP only covered sending to an address on the local network. So the reader cannot see why poisoning one cache entry captures all their internet traffic and not just the packets meant for the router itself; the missing step is that every packet leaving the LAN is sent to the router's MAC address.
fix: one clause: the gateway is the LAN's router, the next hop for every packet bound off the LAN, so its MAC is where all outside traffic goes
reason: The book never teaches that a packet leaving the LAN is addressed to the router's MAC (ch8 ARP covers only sending to an address on the local network, and 'gateway' otherwise appears only inside BGP). p4 does say 'gateway router', but not why poisoning that one entry captures all outside traffic. Prose in p4 is not kept-original, so it can be edited.
judge_fix: In p4: 'the gateway router (the exit every packet bound for outside the LAN is handed to) answers "I do, MAC aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff."' The following sentence 'sends every packet destined for the gateway to the attacker' then reads as all outside traffic.

quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
problem: The caption says speed wins the laptop's cache. Fig 15.4's step 3 ('the cache keeps the freshest claim'), its title ('whoever keeps answering wins') and p4's 'keeps telling it' all say the latest answer wins, so the reader cannot tell what makes the laptop believe the attacker over the real gateway's reply.
fix: make the caption match step 3: the cache keeps the latest answer, so the attacker wins by repeating, not by being fast
reason: The caption belongs to Fig 15.4, a kept-original figure. The inconsistency is real but small: caption says 'faster', drawn step 2 says 'replies first' (consistent), but step 3 and the title say the cache keeps the freshest claim and 'whoever keeps answering wins'. Speed alone does not win, since ARP caches take the latest reply.
judge_fix: Owner call: 'The attacker on the same LAN simply answers ARP queries, and keeps answering, so the laptop's cache settles on the attacker's claim and every packet goes through their machine.'

quote: any modern OS does this with one sysctl
problem: 'sysctl' is never defined, so the reader cannot tell what the single step is that turns the attacker's machine into a forwarder, and stops on the unfamiliar word.
fix: 'with one setting', or a gloss: a single operating-system setting
reason: The caption belongs to Fig 15.4, a kept-original figure. 'sysctl' is never defined anywhere in the book; the meaning survives in context (packet forwarding is one switch) so this is low severity.
judge_fix: Owner call: 'any modern OS does this with one setting'.

quote: requires a separate PUT request before GET, breaking the simplest SSRF pattern
problem: The reader knows GET and PUT (ch11-http) and how SSRF works, but cannot say why a PUT-first rule stops it. The missing step: a simple SSRF only chooses the URL of a plain GET the server sends, so it cannot make the server send the PUT that gets the token first.
fix: a simple SSRF picks only the address of a GET, so it cannot send the PUT that fetches the token
reason: The caption belongs to Fig 15.6, a kept-original figure. The gap is real: the book does not say why a PUT-first rule stops a simple SSRF. The accurate reason (the PUT carries the token request and a plain SSRF only controls the URL of a GET) is not given. The claim itself is factually correct for IMDSv2.
judge_fix: Owner call: '...a session-token-based metadata service whose token comes from a separate PUT request before any GET; a simple SSRF only chooses the address of a GET, so it cannot fetch the token.'

quote: evidence lived on the endpoint, not in network logs: in which process spawned which
problem: The reader knows what a process is and that fork creates one, but nothing says why one process starting another proves an attack. Every other generation in this paragraph gets a concrete case (port 80, Helsinki and Tokyo); this step gets none.
fix: one example, e.g. a web server or a document reader starting a command shell (as Ch 3's shellcode does), which normal use never does
reason: Every other generation in p1 gets a concrete case, but this one gives only 'which process spawned which' with no hint of why that is evidence of attack. The reader knows fork (Part II) and shell-spawning from Chapter 3, so one example suffices.
judge_fix: '...not in network logs: in which process spawned which (a document reader or web server starting a command shell is something normal use never does).'

quote: by reprogramming the PLCs that set the centrifuges' spin speed
problem: The abbreviation PLC is used here and throughout Fig 15.8 with no expansion and no word on what kind of thing it is. It is explained only at p5 ('PLCs, programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves'), two blocks later.
fix: move p5's gloss to this first use
reason: PLC appears first in p3 (and throughout Fig 15.8) with no expansion; grep shows no earlier definition. It is glossed only in p5, two blocks later.
judge_fix: p3: 'by reprogramming the PLCs (programmable logic controllers, the small computers that drive motors and valves) that set the centrifuges' spin speed'. p5: 'Industrial control systems (the computers that run factories, pipelines and power plants, built around PLCs) had been treated as low-priority...'

quote: supply-chain equivalent of Certificate Transparency from Chapter 14: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs), reproducible builds
problem: The reader knows how Certificate Transparency works, but nothing says how SBOMs, reproducible builds or signed build provenance work, or how any of them would have caught an altered build like SUNBURST. The analogy and the three remedies are never connected.
fix: one clause, e.g. that a reproducible build lets anyone rebuild the published source and compare the bytes, so a build altered in secret no longer matches
reason: The insight strip names SBOMs, reproducible builds and signed provenance as the 'equivalent of Certificate Transparency' without saying what any does or how it would expose an altered build like SUNBURST. The glosses exist only later, in Part V, so they are not an answer at this place.
judge_fix: '...Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs, a list of every component inside a program), reproducible builds (anyone can rebuild the published source and compare the bytes, so a build altered in secret no longer matches), signed build provenance (SLSA, sigstore).'

quote: show a further habit: chaining pieces the attacker did not write
problem: The prose groups the book's attacks as data-as-code, confused deputy and a 'chaining' habit (ROP, Stuxnet). Fig 15.9 then gives six patterns: chaining is not one of them, and four of them never appear in the prose. So the reader cannot place ROP and Stuxnet, or square this with p7's claim that 'six structural attack patterns now name every specific exploit in this book'.
fix: p1 names the six patterns and says where chaining (ROP, Stuxnet) sits among them, or that it is a way of combining them
reason: p1 lists data-as-code, a 'further habit' (chaining) and confused deputy, while Fig 15.9 and its caption give six patterns and chaining is not among them. p7 then claims six patterns 'name every specific exploit in this book', so the reader cannot place ROP or Stuxnet. A short clause in p1 removes the tension without touching the figure.
judge_fix: In p1: 'ROP (Chapter 3) and Stuxnet (Section 05) show a further habit, not a pattern of its own: chaining pieces the attacker did not write (existing code fragments, stolen keys, unpatched flaws) into something their authors never anticipated, which is how the patterns below get combined.' Then end the paragraph: 'Fig 15.9 maps all six patterns. Once they have names, every new vulnerability is recognisable as a member of a class, and the defences for that class are ones already understood.'

quote: only then publishes: 30 days after a fix, or at the deadline
problem: The section never says why publishing a bug that is still unfixed on day 90 helps anyone (Fig 15.10 circles it, and the strip only says 'silence' is worse). To this reader it looks like handing attackers a weapon, so the convention's logic cannot be explained back.
fix: one clause: the deadline is what makes vendors fix, attackers may find the bug anyway, and once told, users can protect themselves
reason: p3 and the Fig 15.10 strip say what the deadline does but never why publishing an unfixed bug at day 90 helps. To a newcomer that looks like arming attackers, and the strip only says silence is worse without saying why.
judge_fix: p3: 'and only then publishes: 30 days after a fix, or at the deadline if there is none, because without a deadline a vendor can sit on a bug indefinitely, and users cannot protect themselves from a flaw nobody has told them about.'

quote: FireEye discovered it after spotting unusual traffic on its own network in December 2020.
problem: Unusual traffic is not how FireEye found the breach. Kevin Mandia (Aspen Institute, January 2021) and FireEye's CTO Charles Carmakal both said the first sign was an alert that a second phone had been enrolled in an employee's two-factor login. When staff called the employee, he said he had not registered it. The investigation that started there led to SUNBURST.
fix: "FireEye found it in December 2020, after an alert that a new phone had been enrolled in one employee's two-factor login." Source: Dark Reading, "FireEye's Mandia: 'Severity-Zero Alert' Led to Discovery of SolarWinds Attack" (darkreading.com/threat-intelligence/fireeyes-mandia-severity-zero-alert-led-to-discovery-of-solarwinds-attack).
reason: Checked Mandia's prepared testimony (Senate Intelligence Committee, Feb 2021) and press accounts: FireEye's own breach surfaced through an alert that a second phone had been registered for one employee's two-factor codes; the employee denied it, and the investigation led to SUNBURST. Not 'unusual traffic'. The book's wording is wrong.
judge_fix: FireEye found it in December 2020: tracing an alert that a second phone had been registered to one employee's two-factor login led it to the backdoor. (Source: Kevin Mandia, prepared testimony to the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, 23 Feb 2021; Dark Reading, 'Severity-Zero Alert' interview.)

quote: the BGP and DNS vulnerabilities they had in mind were real
problem: No source puts DNS in the L0pht's 30-minute claim. The Washington Post (Timberg, 'A disaster foretold', 22 June 2015) says the takedown was 'by exploiting flaws in a key Internet routing protocol called BGP'. Space Rogue's own later account names only a BGP flaw that cascaded through routers. DNS seems to come from Mudge's much later remark that BGP was 'at least as big an issue as the DNS issue', which is a comparison with Kaminsky's 2008 bug.
fix: "They were not joking: the BGP flaw they had in mind was real, and the testimony was carried verbatim into the Senate's published hearing record." Sources: Washington Post, Net of Insecurity part 3 (2015); Cris Thomas interview, lieu.house.gov/media-center/in-the-news/i-spoke-hacker-who-could-have-taken-down-internet-30-minutes.
reason: The hearing itself named no flaw. The BGP link comes from Washington Post 2015 and Space Rogue's later interviews; no source puts DNS in the 30-minute claim. Cheap one-word-class repair.
judge_fix: They were not joking: the BGP flaw they had in mind was real, and the testimony was carried verbatim into the Senate's published hearing record. (Sources: Washington Post, 'A disaster foretold', 22 Jun 2015; Cris Thomas interview, lieu.house.gov in-the-news.)

quote: It was the first time the American government heard, on the record,
problem: Overclaims 'first'. On 26 September 1983 Neal Patrick of the 414s testified to a House committee on how easily he had broken into Los Alamos and Sloan-Kettering systems. That is a hacker telling Congress on the record how attackers see systems. The Washington Post calls the L0pht testimony 'among the most audacious of a rising chorus of warnings delivered in the 1990s', not the first.
fix: "It was the starkest warning the American government had yet heard, on the record, that adversaries thought about computer systems differently ..." (the rest unchanged). Sources: Wikipedia 'The 414s' (House testimony, 26 Sept 1983); Washington Post 2015 (as above).
reason: 'First time' is an overclaim: Neal Patrick of the 414s testified to a House subcommittee on how easily systems were broken into on 26 Sept 1983, and the Post calls the L0pht hearing one of a 'rising chorus' of 1990s warnings. A softer superlative keeps the sentence's point.
judge_fix: It was the starkest warning the American government had yet heard, on the record, that adversaries thought about computer systems differently from the people who built them, that there was a discipline of _misuse_ with its own working theory, and that the systems the country was beginning to depend on had not been built with that discipline in mind.

quote: simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway
problem: The caption (ch15-network-p5) brings back the 'first answer wins' mechanism that §4g corrected. The ledger fixed fig 15.4 and ch15-network-p4 to 'keeps answering', because RFC 826 overwrites a cache entry with each later claim. The drawing now says 'the cache keeps the freshest claim', while its caption still says the attacker wins by answering faster.
fix: Caption: "The attacker on the same LAN keeps answering ARP queries with its own MAC address, so the laptop's cache always holds the forged entry and every packet is redirected through the attacker's machine." Source: RFC 826 (merge flag updates existing entries); UNDER.md §4g Part IV fig 15.4 entry.
reason: Real. The fig 15.4 caption (kept original) says the attacker 'simply answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway', which brings back the first-answer-wins mechanism that UNDER.md section 4g corrected in the drawing and in ch15-network-p4 ('keeps answering', RFC 826 overwrites on later claims). Caption now contradicts the drawing ('the cache keeps the freshest claim'). Kept-original, so only the owner can change it.
judge_fix: Caption sentence: 'The attacker on the same LAN keeps answering ARP queries with its own MAC address, so the laptop's cache always ends up holding the forged entry and every packet is redirected through their machine.' (Source: RFC 826; UNDER.md 4g fig 15.4 entry.)

quote: AWS now mandates IMDSv2
problem: Overclaim, both in the caption and in the drawn line 'mandatory on new instances'. AWS's November 2023 announcement made only instance types released from mid-2024 IMDSv2-only by default, and IMDSv1 can still be turned back on. Older instance types still launch with v1 unless the account blocks it with the account-level setting. Amazon Linux 2023 disables v1 by default. 'Default' is accurate. 'Mandates' is not.
fix: Caption: "at the cloud platform, AWS now defaults to IMDSv2, a session-token-based metadata service ...". Drawn line: "(the default on new instance types)". Source: AWS News Blog, 'Amazon EC2 Instance Metadata Service IMDSv2 by default' (Nov 2023); AWS EC2 User Guide, 'Transition to using IMDSv2'.
reason: Real overclaim in a kept-original figure (caption and drawn line). AWS's Nov 2023 change made only newly released instance types IMDSv2-only by default (from mid-2024), with an account-level default available; IMDSv1 still launches on older types. 'Default' is right, 'mandates' / 'mandatory on new instances' is not.
judge_fix: Caption: 'at the cloud platform, AWS now defaults to IMDSv2, a session-token-based metadata service that requires a separate PUT request before GET, ...'. Drawn line: '(the default on new instance types)'. Source: AWS News Blog, 'EC2 IMDSv2 by default' (Nov 2023); EC2 User Guide, 'Transition to using IMDSv2'.

quote: Stuxnet infected ~100K machines but did damage on perhaps a hundred.
problem: No source supports 'perhaps a hundred', and it is probably off by an order of magnitude. The damage happened at one site, Natanz. ISIS (Albright, Brannan, Walrond, 22 Dec 2010) estimates that about 1,000 of roughly 9,000 IR-1 centrifuges were destroyed and replaced. A reader will take 'machines damaged' as about a hundred.
fix: "Stuxnet infected ~100K computers but did damage at one site: about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz." Source: isis-online.org, 'Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant?' (2010).
reason: Real, in kept-original Fig 15.8. 'Perhaps a hundred' machines has no source; the ISIS estimate (Albright et al., Dec 2010) is about 1,000 of roughly 9,000 IR-1 centrifuges destroyed at Natanz. Finding 31 is the same point.
judge_fix: 'no matching PLC: lie dormant. Stuxnet infected ~100K computers but did damage at one site: about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz.' (Source: isis-online.org, 'Did Stuxnet Take Out 1,000 Centrifuges at the Natanz Enrichment Plant?', 2010.)

quote: intrusion detection system (IDS, early 2000s) answered that
problem: Intrusion detection is older than this date suggests. Denning's model is from 1987, and commercial network IDS shipped in 1996–98 (ISS RealSecure, Snort in December 1998). By June 2003 Gartner was already calling IDS 'dead'. Zero trust's 'late 2010s' is also late: Kindervag coined the term at Forrester in 2010, and BeyondCorp was described in 2014, as the figure's own strip says. Fig 15.7 carries the same two labels.
fix: Prose: "(IDS, late 1990s)" and "*Zero-trust architecture* (2010s)". Fig 15.7: "late 1990s: inspect what got in" and "2010s: trust no position". Sources: Denning, IEEE TSE 1987; Snort 1.0 release (1998); Kindervag, Forrester 'No More Chewy Centers' (2010).
reason: Network IDS was commercial by 1996-98 (ISS RealSecure, Snort Dec 1998), and the figure's own strip names Snort, so 'early 2000s' is wrong; Gartner called IDS dead in 2003. The 'late 2010s' for zero trust is fine as the adoption era (NIST SP 800-207, 2020), so only the IDS date changes. Fig 15.7 is not a kept original.
judge_fix: Prose ch15-defense-p1: '(IDS, late 1990s)'. Fig 15.7 desc: 'In the late 1990s an intrusion detection system inspects the traffic that got through.' Drawn label: 'late 1990s: inspect what got in'. Leave the zero-trust date.

quote: for vulnerabilities reported through these channels
problem: The sentence says Apple, Google and Microsoft pay through HackerOne, Bugcrowd and YesWeHack. All three run their own programs: Apple Security Bounty (security.apple.com), Google VRP (bughunters.google.com) and the Microsoft Bounty Program (MSRC). The platforms serve many other companies.
fix: "*HackerOne*, *Bugcrowd*, *YesWeHack* are the major platforms, and Apple, Google and Microsoft run programs of their own; between them they pay independent researchers (from about $1K to $1M or more per finding, depending on severity)."
reason: Low. As written the sentence implies Apple, Google and Microsoft pay via HackerOne/Bugcrowd/YesWeHack; each runs its own program. A short repair is true and keeps the length.
judge_fix: *HackerOne*, *Bugcrowd*, *YesWeHack* are the major platforms, and Apple, Google, Microsoft and most major tech companies also run programs of their own; between them they pay independent researchers (from about $1K to $1M or more per finding, depending on severity) for the vulnerabilities they report.

quote: now the laptop sends every packet destined for the gateway to the attacker instead
problem: Poisoning only the laptop's cache gives the attacker one direction. The gateway still sends its replies straight to the laptop. A full man in the middle (arpspoof, ettercap) also tells the gateway that the laptop's IP is at the attacker's MAC. As written, a reader will think one forged answer makes the attacker see both sides of the conversation.
fix: After "...to the attacker instead." add: "It tells the gateway the same lie about the laptop, so the replies come through it too."
reason: Low. One forged answer to the laptop gives the attacker only the laptop-to-gateway half; replies still go straight to the laptop. p4 then calls the attacker a transparent intermediary and p5 'MITM', which p2 defines as relaying both directions. A one-sentence fix in the prose (the caption is kept-original and need not change).
judge_fix: After 'to the attacker instead.' add: 'It tells the gateway the same lie about the laptop, so the replies come through it too.'

quote: for that call site when it built the program for that call site
problem: A phrase is duplicated: 'for that call site' appears twice in one clause. This is not a fact error, but it is a slip a reader will stop on.
fix: "the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site when it built the program."
reason: Verified in text: 'for that call site when it built the program for that call site' repeats the phrase. A slip the reader will stop on. Fix also removes the per-call-site claim that does not hold for MSVC CFG (see 17).
judge_fix: the target address must be one the compiler recorded as valid for that call when it built the program. A function pointer overwritten with a gadget address fails the check, because the gadget is not on the list of valid targets.

problem: ch15-mindset-p1 says 'the first time the American government heard, on the record' how attackers think. Neal Patrick of the 414s testified on hacking before a House subcommittee in September 1983, so 'first time' looks overstated.
reason: Same as finding 3; 'first time' is an overclaim (414s testified to the House on 26 Sept 1983).
judge_fix: As finding 3: 'It was the starkest warning the American government had yet heard, on the record, that adversaries thought about computer systems differently ...' (rest unchanged).

problem: ch15-mindset-p1 says 'the BGP and DNS vulnerabilities they had in mind were real'. The 1998 testimony did not name the flaws. Later accounts (Mudge, e.g. Washington Post 2015) point to BGP. I could not find a source for DNS.
reason: Same as finding 2; no source puts DNS in the L0pht claim, only BGP (Washington Post 2015, Space Rogue).
judge_fix: As finding 2: 'the BGP flaw they had in mind was real'.

problem: ch15-memory-p3: 'valid for that call site' / 'the call site's allow-list' fits Clang's type-based CFI. MSVC's Control Flow Guard, also named here, keeps one program-wide set of valid targets (any address-taken function start), not a list per call site. The gadget example still holds, because a mid-function gadget is not a function start.
reason: Low. MSVC CFG keeps a program-wide set of valid targets, not a per-call-site list, though Clang's type-based CFI is closer to per-call. The wording is cheaply made true alongside the typo fix in 13.
judge_fix: Use the wording in finding 13 ('valid for that call', 'the list of valid targets'); no separate edit.

problem: ch15-network-p5 (caption): 'answers ARP queries faster than the legitimate gateway'. Most ARP implementations overwrite the cache with the latest reply, and many also accept replies nobody asked for. Spoofing works by sending forged replies again and again, not by winning a race. The kept-original Fig 15.4 (step 3) already says so, and the caption contradicts it.
reason: Same as finding 5: the kept-original Fig 15.4 caption contradicts the drawing and the section 4g correction.
judge_fix: As finding 5: 'The attacker on the same LAN keeps answering ARP queries with its own MAC address, so the laptop's cache always ends up holding the forged entry ...'

problem: ch15-network-p4/p5: poisoning only the laptop's cache sends just laptop-to-gateway traffic through the attacker. The gateway's replies still go straight to the laptop's real MAC. A real two-way man-in-the-middle also poisons the gateway's cache for the laptop's IP. The text calls the one-way case a 'transparent intermediary' and says 'the attacker is now MITM' (p2 defines MITM as relaying each side's traffic to the other).
reason: Same as finding 10: the one-way poisoning is described as a full MITM. Repair belongs in the p4 prose, not the kept-original caption.
judge_fix: As finding 10: after 'to the attacker instead.' add 'It tells the gateway the same lie about the laptop, so the replies come through it too.'

problem: ch15-web-p5 'AWS now mandates IMDSv2': overstated. Since mid-2024, only newly released EC2 instance types run IMDSv2-only by default, and accounts can set IMDSv2 as their default. IMDSv1 is still available on most instance types and launches. Kept-original fig-15-6 says the same ('mandatory on new instances'), so report it as kind kept-original, low severity.
reason: Same as finding 6: 'AWS now mandates IMDSv2' (caption) and 'mandatory on new instances' (drawing) overclaim in kept-original Fig 15.6.
judge_fix: As finding 6: 'AWS now defaults to IMDSv2' and drawn line '(the default on new instance types)'.

problem: ch15-web-p4 'SSRF became one of the most common high-impact vulnerabilities': OWASP 2021 added SSRF (A10) on the strength of its community survey, and its incidence rate in the OWASP data was low (about 2.7%). 'High-impact' holds. 'One of the most common' is doubtful.
reason: Low. OWASP 2021 added SSRF as A10 from its community survey, with a low measured incidence (about 2.7%); 'one of the most common' is not supported while 'high-impact' is. Swap the superlative.
judge_fix: *Server-Side Request Forgery* (SSRF) became one of the most dangerous vulnerabilities of the cloud era.

problem: ch15-defense-p1 dates the IDS generation to the 'early 2000s', but the same figure's How it works strip names Snort, which was released in 1998. Commercial IDS products (e.g. ISS RealSecure, 1997) and the research behind them (Denning's IDES, 1980s) are older. 'Late 1990s' would be safer.
